blocks.p: Dear Stephen, you kept the Mars relays for a hundred and forty years, so you’ll know this better than I can tell it. Some nights the returns came back with weather on them. You logged it as weather. So did I, for longer than I like to admit. If a Renewal has tidied this out of your head, do one thing for me: the next time the weather comes, listen to it.
The Sedge went into the mud at Reedmouth with Teo Thorne at her stick, and it was Sol who had put him there.

Word had come up the river that morning. Reedmouth was the Thorne fueling pier where the Wend spread into the sea, a day downriver by water and forty minutes by air, with a chapel outpost and one clerk, and a pump-keeper named Orrin Vale, baptized at Jory’s in the spring, had seized on the pier in front of the clerk. The clerk had put it on the relay. The circuit priest’s ship was due on the morning tide. The priest had no warrant; but a man lying confused on a pier after a fit, with a kind voice over him asking whether he would like to come aboard and be seen to, would say yes. Sol had heard that yes a thousand times and signed under it.

Tobin was on the Kestrel, two days out. The barge would take a day each way. The Sedge, the line’s one flyer, sat in the yard loaded with Pearl frames and glass for the Reedmouth chapel, waiting on Hollis.
Teo had asked for the run at breakfast, with Sol at the table.
“No,” Lyda had said, without looking up from her slate. “Not the delta. Not in the rains, and not with your clearance still blank where the name goes. When Hollis is back.”
“Two days.”
“Then it’s two days.”
Sol had said nothing at the table. He thought about it all day, carrying bales, until the thought wore smooth. At dusk he found Teo at the foot of the loft ladder.
“Could you fly her?”
Teo looked up. “The Sedge? In my sleep.” He grinned. “Why?”
Sol told him about Orrin Vale. He watched the boy’s face change while he told it, and he knew what he was doing, and did it.
“Lyda said no,” Teo said. It was not an objection. It was a boy laying a fact on the table to see what the man across from him would do with it.
“I know what she said.” Sol heard his own voice, gentle and certain, the voice of a thousand wharves. “I’m asking.”
Teo looked at him a moment longer, with the face he had worn on top of the bales with his arms out. Then he went to find a hand for the crate.

The Sedge lifted off in the last of the light with a loader named Hob Carrow in the second seat. Sol stood under the eaves of the dye shed and watched her running lights go out across the reeds into the rain. He told himself that a man would have been on a ship by morning. It was true. He went on telling himself.

Forty minutes later she had not called in from Reedmouth. At fifty the yard launch rang its bell, and Lyda came down the counting-house stair with her coat half on and stopped on the bottom step and looked at him, and did not need to be told anything.

They found the Sedge by her one lamp still burning, a mile short of the pier, nose down in the mudflats where the river braided out among the reed islands. She had come in flat and fast and slid, and the mud had taken her nose and broken her back, and the crate had gone through the forward bulkhead and burst. Gilt frames stood up out of the brown water at angles. Glass lay everywhere in the lamplight, so that the whole flat glittered like a floor someone had dropped a Pearl on.

Hob Carrow sat in the mud beside the hull with his right arm held against his chest, bent where no arm bends. Teo’s head was on his thigh. The boy was asleep, the deep slack sleep that came after, with his brow split and his left wrist swelling. Hob had dragged him out through the hatch, he said. He said it to Lyda, who had gone down on her knees in the mud with her hand on her brother’s hair and had not said a word.

“He said it was going bright.” Hob’s voice was flat with shock. “Took his hands off and started putting her down, careful, the way they teach. Got her half down. Then he cried out and went stiff as a plank, and I had the stick, and I don’t fly.” He looked at his arm as if it belonged to the hull. “He talked, after. Shepherd, and something. There wasn’t anybody to cover my ears for me, so I listened.” He looked past Lyda, to where Sol stood knee deep in the brown water with the lamp. “He said the bishop asked him.”
Lyda did not look up.

Lucan set Hob’s arm in two places and wrote it down. Teo slept in the back room with his wrist splinted and his brow stitched, and Lyda sat with him until his breathing told her what she needed, and then came out onto the infirmary stair, where Sol stood because he could not have sat.
“You heard me say no to him,” she said.
“Yes.”
“And you asked him anyway.”
“Yes.”
She was quiet a moment, with one hand on the rail. The rain came down past the stair lamp in long bright lines.

“Jory’s taken the barge down,” she said. “He’ll have Orrin Vale under a load of wet reed by tomorrow night and up the river the day after. That’s how long it would have taken if you’d come to me this morning. I’d have said no to you too, and then I’d have sent the barge.” She looked at him for the first time. “You didn’t come to me. You went to a boy who’d fly into the sun if you asked him, because you knew what I’d say and you knew what he’d say. That’s not asking, Bishop. That’s signing.”
Sol said nothing. There was no part of it he could have argued with.

“Hob Carrow’s arm is in two pieces. The Sedge is in the mud with her back broken, and I don’t own another. A chapel’s Pearls are lying in the reeds in a thousand bits, and the church’s freight is what keeps this line alive, and that clerk will have it on the relay by breakfast: a Thorne flyer, a Thorne trainee with a history of falls, down in the delta with a hand hurt.” Her voice did not rise once. “Weir will have it with his tea.”
“I’m sorry, Lyda.”

“I know you are. You were sorry about Davi Coyle, too.” She went past him up the stair, and stopped at the top without turning round. “He’d have gone anyway, one day, to something. I’ve known that since he was nine. I’d have liked it to be his own idea.”

The circuit priest’s ship had lain at the bar through the rains, as ships on the Wend did in that season and as anyone on the river could have told Sol if he had asked, and came into Reedmouth a day late to an empty pier. Orrin Vale came up the river on the third day under a load of wet reed, and never knew that a flyer had gone into the mud for him. Nobody told him.

Teo went to see Hob Carrow on the fourth day, with his wrist splinted and the stitches black in his brow. Sol walked with him as far as the loader’s door. Through the window he saw the boy stand in front of Hob’s chair and say something, and Hob look at him a long while, and then at the arm strapped across his own chest, and answer.
Teo came out white.
“He says I put her down careful,” he said. “He says he told Weir so.” He walked a few steps along the boardwalk and stopped. “He says he won’t go up with me again. Not ever. He was nice about it.”
He said nothing else all the way home, and Sol did not ask him to.
Ansel Weir came up the counting-house stair the next evening with his slate. Sol was at the long table checking bale weights, because Lyda did not want him on the wharf, and he began to rise.
“Stay, Bishop,” Lyda said, without looking up. “You’ll want to hear what you cost.”

Weir had gone under the hood in the autumn, first, as she had promised him, and the slack at his jowls was gone, so that his mild pale eyes seemed set into a younger face from somewhere else. He laid the slate on her desk.

“Reedmouth put it on the relay,” he said. “And Hob Carrow came to me with a statement. The boy said it was going bright. He cried out and went stiff as a plank. Afterward he talked. That’s the chapel film, Lyda, word for word.”
“He put her down short in the rains. He’s sixteen.”

“He has a great many falls,” Weir said gently. “In twelve years I’ve never written one down. But the circuit priest came into Reedmouth to a broken flyer and a story, and he’s asked me why the registry has nothing on the boy. The quarter goes up the line in a week. What would you like me to put?”
“Put that I asked him to fly,” Sol said.
“Oh, I’ve put that, Your Grace. Hob was very clear.”
Lyda laid her pen down.

“Nothing,” she said. “You’ll put nothing about my brother. Not the falls, not the flyer, not Hob, not ever. And you go under first. Not just this year. Every time, for as long as that hood stands, and the parts come in my holds or they don’t come at all.”
Weir considered it. Sol watched him, and understood with a cold that went down into his fingers that the man was not hesitating. He was enjoying being asked.
“Every time,” Weir said.

At the door he turned back, as he always did. “I’ll keep the boy off the registry, Lyda. You know I keep my word.” His pale eyes went to Sol. “Your Thorne hand is another matter. I file every soul on this river, and every ship’s list before she clears. That’s the chapel’s. You can’t buy it.” He smiled mildly. “I wouldn’t sell it.”
When his steps had gone down the stair, Lyda picked up her pen.
“That’s the hood, for as long as it stands, to keep my brother off a list,” she said. “That’s what a man on a pier cost. Check your weights, Bishop.”
The only door to heaven on Philippa was in the cellar under Imre Lucan’s infirmary, and the doctor kept it locked with a padlock he had bought at the ship chandler’s.

Three weeks later, Sol went down the stair behind him with the lamp. The steps were stone, worn hollow in the middle, and steep, and lately he had begun to take stairs the way old men took them in the archival images: one hand on the wall, a small pause at each step, as if to ask the knee whether it agreed. Teo had told him so, cheerfully, at supper in front of everyone. You go down stairs like my sister’s accountant.

There was grey all through his hair now, coarse and wiry, so that in the shaving glass he sometimes saw a stranger and had to wait for the stranger to become him. Ten months dark. Ten years paid, though the curve in the grey ledger with Sol’s name on it had already begun to bend, as Jory’s had.

The cellar was cold and smelled of dust and machine oil. The relay stood against the back wall, a tall grey cabinet with the church’s gold sunburst on its door, humming. The church had put it down here because people died in infirmaries, and one line from the deathbeds to the gate was cheaper than twenty. Beside it Lucan had built a bench out of packing crates: a board of his own making, a coil of fine silver wire, a cot, and the thick cloth-bound book he wrote everything in.
Teo was sitting cross-legged on the cot, waiting.
“You’re late,” he said. “He said eighth hour.”

“Brother Sol is ten years older than he was when he came off the Kestrel,” Lucan said, without turning. “He’s allowed to be late.” He touched the board, and the air above it filled with the gold climb of an ascension log. “Sit down, Tarren. I want you to see this before the boy starts showing off.”
Sol sat on a crate. He was glad of it.

“Forty-one ascensions from Philippa and the near stations since the turn of the year,” Lucan said. “Eleven not received. Four of those were the relay; it’s old, and the damp gets in. Seven came back with this on them.” He opened the top of the climb with two fingers, as the young technician on Serenity had done, and the flat line where the gold stopped spread into a fine grey fringe. “A failed backup sits in the relay about three weeks before it falls apart. The circuit technician wipes the residue as interference. I started copying it.”
“On Serenity they told me to call it hardware.”
“Everything is hardware, at some level.” Lucan’s mouth moved slightly. “The question is whose.”
He touched the board again, and sound came out of the cabinet.

Sol knew it at once: the dry endless hiss of a line with nothing on it, and under the hiss, so low he had to lean toward it, a rising and a falling and a pause and a rising again. Under the ice of Europa it had sounded like the responses in a cathedral heard through a closed door. It sounded like that now. He felt the skin tighten on his arms.

“Speakers give you that,” Lucan said. “So I tried it the other way. The colonial implants have a service contact beside the coin, so a technician can reach the hardware without opening anything. I ran a lead from the board to my own and let the Halo decode it. It can’t. It gives up and passes the signal through raw, straight to the hearing.” He paused. “I listened for an hour. I heard weather.”
“And Teo?”
“Teo,” said Lucan, “heard something else.”
“I heard people,” Teo said.

He said it with his chin up and his hands on his knees. His Halo had been put in at nine by a contract implanter on the Thorne docks, a cheap colonial model; Sol could see the small raised seam of the contact beside the coin. His own had no such seam. Sion did not let anyone service a bishop.
“Does your sister know you’re here?” Sol said.
“She knows I’m at the doctor’s.”
“Does she know why?”
Teo grinned.

“Then take him home,” Sol said. He had stood on the infirmary stair the night of the Sedge and been told what asking this boy for anything was, and he had heard it every night since. “He was in the mud at Reedmouth three weeks ago. Fear brings his seizures on. So does sleeplessness. Not without Lyda.”
“It’s my head,” Teo said. “Let it be good for something.”

“And my wire,” said Lucan, “and he’s had it in twice without you, Tarren. I asked you down to hear, not to vote.” He uncoiled the lead. “I know what brings them on. I’ve known what his fainting was since he was ten; his sister only thinks I don’t. Sound doesn’t. This is sound. I’ll keep my hand on the lead.” He looked at Teo. “Did you sleep?”
“Like a stone.”
“He’s lying,” Lucan said to Sol, “but not by much.”

Sol did not go. He wanted to hear; he knew it in himself as plainly as he knew the thumb behind his eye, and he did not trust it. He moved his crate to the head of the cot, where he could reach the lead.
“If he goes pale,” he said, “it comes out.”

Teo lay back. Lucan bent over him, found the seam with a fingertip, and slid the fine needle at the end of the lead into it with a small sure movement. He opened his book on his knee and laid a watch beside it.
“Go on,” he said.
For a while Teo said nothing. His face was intent and still, the face of someone straining after voices through a wall.
“It’s far off,” Teo said. “Like a crowd in the next hall.” His brow creased. “No. They’re saying something together. One of them starts it and the rest come in after.”
“What are they saying?”
“Our Father,” Teo said.
Sol went cold.

“Our Father in heaven.” Teo’s voice had dropped, the way voices drop in a church. “Hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come.” He stopped, listening. “They say that twice. Your kingdom come. Your kingdom come. Like they mean it more the second time.”
Lucan’s pencil moved. “He’s heard you say it.”
“Every week,” Sol said. His voice did not sound like his own.
“Your will be done,” Teo said, “on earth as it is in heaven.” And then, very quietly, with a little catch in it, as though repeating exactly what he heard: “Deliver us. Deliver us from evil.”
Sol looked at the gold sunburst on the cabinet door.

They were in heaven. That was what he could not get past. They were in the City of the Throne, where the street was gold and no one ever wept, the City he had described to grieving families all his life, and they were standing somewhere in it, all together, praying to a Father in heaven. As if they knew, every one of them, that the place they were standing was not it.
“There’s one by herself,” Teo said. “Closer. A woman. She says the same thing over and over, the same way every time. It goes up at the end.”
And Teo said it, with the lift, exactly: “Tell him we’re so happy.”
Sol knew the voice before he knew he knew it. He had heard it on his knees in a chapel the size of a closet, under the ice, with the Pearl glowing gold in front of him.

“That’s on top, though,” Teo said. “Something comes down over her, bright, like looking straight at a lamp, and she says that. But underneath she’s still saying the other thing. She’s been saying it a long time, I think. It’s worn smooth.” He turned his head a little on the cot. “Tell him not to come.”
Lucan had stopped writing. He touched the board, and a line of plain grey text rose beside the gold. “This fragment carries an origin flag. It isn’t Diaspora. Inner colonies. Europa.”
“Serenity,” Sol said. “The old south dome.”
Lucan looked at him for a long moment. “How could you possibly know that?”

So Sol told him, badly, out of order: the infirmary of the lower workings, the big miner under the pressure wrap. Is it far? The mother who had gone up through a breach in the old south dome while he was at school. The wife patting his hand. She’s very happy there. And Joss Arden, with almost no voice left: That’s what she says.

“For a hundred and thirty years,” Sol said, “he went to the Pearl every week and she told him she was happy. And underneath it, all that time, she was telling him not to come. I think he heard it. I think he was trying to tell me, and I didn’t know how to listen.”
“His ascension failed,” Lucan said slowly.
“Four times. The vessel could not be resolved.”
“Then he was refused.”
“Or he was told not to come,” Sol said, “and he listened.”
The pencil scratched. In the cabinet the hiss rose and fell.
“They’re louder,” Teo said. His face had gone pale and fixed, and his hands had closed on the blanket. “They’ve started something else. I don’t know this one. How long. They keep saying how long.”
“Teo,” Sol said.

“How long, O Lord, holy and true.” The words came slowly, as if spelled out from a great distance. “How long before you judge. Something about blood. Now something about white. Someone’s giving them white clothes. And telling them to rest. To rest a little longer.”
“Take it out,” Sol said.
“Another minute,” Lucan said, watching the watch, with his hand over the lead.
“A little longer,” Teo said. “Rest a little longer, until...”
His voice stopped.
Sol had seen it in a market on Mars and on the floor of the dye shed. The boy’s face emptied all at once, as though whoever lived in it had stepped out.

Sol had the doctor’s hand off the lead before Lucan could look up from the watch. He drew the needle out of the seam in one motion, the way he had watched it go in, and then Teo gave a cry like cloth tearing, and went rigid. His back arched. His arms locked against his chest, and his head pressed back.
Then the jerking began.

The cot rocked on the stone. Sol was on his knees before he remembered his knees. Lucan was rolling the boy onto his side, away from the edge, not holding him down, only keeping him there. Sol pulled off his coat and wadded it between Teo’s head and the frame of the cot, where it was striking.
“Time,” Lucan said.
“Eighth hour, nineteen.” Sol did not know how he had it. He had looked at the watch without deciding to.

It was never as long as it seemed. Sol knelt with his hand on the blanket an inch from the boy’s head, as he had knelt in the dye shed, and listened to the cot knock against the stone, and behind it the hiss in the cabinet, a great many people very far away still saying something together.
The spasms slowed, and came further apart, and stopped. Teo lay on Sol’s coat with blood at the corner of his mouth, dragging the air in as if it had to be hauled up out of a well.
“A minute and fifty,” Lucan said quietly, and wrote it down.
There were footsteps on the stair.

Sol knew them: quick, light, a little uneven on the third step. Lyda Thorne stood on the bottom step with her coat still buttoned and a covered dish in one hand, and looked at her brother on the cot, and at the silver wire on the floor, and at Sol.
She set the dish down on the stair, carefully, as though it mattered where it went. Then she crossed the cellar and knelt by the cot and put her hand on Teo’s hair.
“Hey,” she said. “Hey, Teo. It’s me.”
His lips moved. Lyda did not cover his ears, or her own. In all the worlds Sol had lived in, he had never seen anyone kneel beside one of the infected and lean closer.
“A little longer,” Teo whispered, thick and slurred. “Rest a little longer. Until the number...” A long breath. “Lyd?”
“I’m here.”
“They’re all in white,” he said, and closed his eyes, and slept.

They carried him up to the narrow bed in the infirmary’s back room, where, since the day in the dye shed, he had slept off three more seizures, the last of them with mud still in his hair. Lucan checked the boy’s pulse and tongue and pupils, pronounced him sound, and wrote that down too.
Lyda had not said a word on the stair. She said one now.
“Whose wire?”
“Mine,” Lucan said. He did not look up from the book. “Tarren told us no. I overruled him; it was my relay and my wire, and the boy was set on it. When it started, Tarren had it out before I did.”
Lyda looked at Sol once, quickly, the way she checked a figure, and back at the doctor.
“You knew what he was.”
“Since he was ten.”

“Six years.” Her voice did not rise. “Six years you’ve kept him off every record on this river and let me think it was me doing it. You did it so you’d have him when you wanted him. You’d sign anything for an answer, Imre.”

“Very likely.” Lucan closed the book. He was white about the mouth, but he did not look away from her. “I won’t wire him again. You have my word. But I want a second listener before I trust any of this. Someone with a live Halo. Mine heard weather, and his heard people, and the only difference between us that I can find is that mine still has the hum on it, and his has been dark for months.” He went out.
Lyda sat on the edge of the bed. Sol stood in the doorway.
“Dark,” Lyda said.
She did not turn round. Sol watched her take the word and turn it over and find what was under it.
“Since when?”
“Galatia,” Sol said. “A stock pond at Highfold, the last evening.”
“He asked you.”
“Yes.”
“And asked you not to tell me.” It was not a question. “Twelve years I kept his secret from the whole river, Bishop. It never once crossed my mind that anyone would keep one of his from me.”
“I promised him,” Sol said.

“I know you did. That’s why he asked you and not the doctor.” She still did not look at him. “You’ve sat at my table with it since you came home. You’ve watched me tell him to put a coat on.” She was quiet a moment. “You decided I couldn’t carry it. I’ve carried him for twelve years.”
It went in where it was meant to. He did not look for an answer.
“I’m sorry, Lyda,” he said.
She was quiet for a while. Her hand had gone back to his hair without her seeming to notice.
“What did he hear?” she said.
He told her, as plainly as he could. She listened the way she listened to her shipmasters’ reports, with no expression at all.
“Dead people,” she said. “Praying. To what? They’re already there. They’re standing in front of it.”
“Not to what they’re standing in front of,” Sol said.
She did not answer that.
“I don’t believe a word of it,” Lyda said. Then, after a moment, still not looking at him: “Tell me the rest anyway. When he’s awake. I want to hear it again.”

Lucan was at his desk in the front room with the lamp turned low. He had laid the transcript beside the log, Teo’s words in one column and the rises and falls of the signal drawn in pencil in the other, joined with fine straight lines.

“Every syllable lands on a peak,” he said, without looking up. “Every pause lands on a trough. The boy was on his back looking at the ceiling. He couldn’t see the trace.” He laid the pencil down. “I’m a physician, Tarren. I’ve never had to know what a soul is. But I know a sixteen-year-old can’t keep time with a signal he can’t see, for nine minutes, to the syllable.”
“And the woman? The bright thing over her?”

“Your machine can’t read whatever this is. It’s been editing these people for centuries, and it can’t find this to take it out. So it does the only thing it can.” He tapped the column where Teo had said something comes down over her. “It paints over it. We’re so happy here. It’s a coat of paint.”
“And underneath,” Sol said.
“Underneath,” said Lucan, “your heaven is full of people who won’t go along with it.”

Sol took the grey notebook to his room under the eaves. The voices in the cellar had been speaking of a throne and the ones before it, and there was only one book in the copy full of thrones. He had read it once, quickly, and been frightened. He went toward it through the letters, and on the way a line stopped him, because Stephen’s pen had pressed so hard there that the words stood up in ridges under his thumb.
And no wonder, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light. So it is no great thing if his servants also disguise themselves as servants of righteousness.
In the margin, very small: This one came back in a seizure. I had a blank where the name was.

He did not know why the hand had pressed so hard there. He sat a moment with his thumb on the ridges, and then he turned on. He went through the last book page by page until he came to the sixth chapter, and stopped.

There was a space. Half a page, left empty. In the margin beside it, smaller than the rest, as if written at the end of a long night, Stephen had put a note: Gone. Water got this page sometime in the last few centuries. I’ll come back to it.
He had not come back to it. He had gone to a market on Mars instead.

Sol unwrapped the other book and found the place by counting from the end: a brown leaf, stiff and cockled, its ink long since run into a mottled stain like the shadow of leaves on water. He had looked at it before and seen nothing.
He tilted the lamp until the light lay almost flat across the page and, holding in his mind the words a boy had spoken on a cot in a cellar, looked again.

How long. There. A ghost of it, the shapes of the letters rising out of the stain where the ink had lain heavier. Holy and true. A white robe. And lower, almost lost at the crumbled edge: rest a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be complete, who were to be killed as they themselves had been.
He read it three times. Then he sat with the page in the lamplight and did not move.

Teo had not known these words. Sol had not known them. Stephen had left them a space and a promise, and gone to his death with the space still empty. And somewhere beyond the dark and the gold, in a city where no one was supposed to want anything but the next thing, people in white robes had been saying them at the gate, over and over, for as long as it took someone to listen.
He opened the grey notebook to the empty half page and took up the pencil.

His hand was not as steady as it had been when he came to Philippa. The letters came out small and crooked under Stephen’s note, and when he came to killed he had to stop and wait before he could go on. They were the first words he had ever added to the book.
When he had finished he turned the lamp down, and sat in the dark, and did as Stephen had asked.
He listened to the weather.
